What Dr. Poston says to focus on Built from Dr. Brad Poston's Renal II: Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (slides + narration). He is a family-medicine physician and says these conditions are rare but heavily tested (quizzes and Step exams), so know when to suspect RPGN, the light microscopy findings, and the three IF patterns. He repeats that immunofluorescence is how you separate the subtypes, and that exams give an ANCA result (c- or p-) to pick the diagnosis. Practice questions sit at the end of each section; the summary table is last. beyond source = standard teaching I added; corrected = source slip fixed.

1. Overview: When To Think RPGN

Clinical picture

  • Rapid, progressive loss of renal function over weeks to months: falling eGFR, rising creatinine, oliguria, then electrolyte abnormalities as GFR drops.
  • Nephritic urinalysis: hematuria (macroscopic, pink/brown urine, is more common; microscopic also occurs), dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, and proteinuria that is usually non-nephrotic (<3.5 g/24 h).
  • For scale: diabetic nephropathy progresses over 20–30 years; RPGN over weeks to months.
Transcript slip correctedThe narration says the urinalysis shows "a nephrotic picture." His slide (and the physiology) say nephritic: hematuria, RBC casts, and proteinuria below the nephrotic range.

It is a clinicopathologic diagnosis

  • Signs, symptoms and labs strongly suggest it, but you need a renal biopsy to confirm and to sort the subtype.
  • Early treatment is critical (Section 3).

Three things to learn

  1. Signs and symptoms (above).
  2. Light microscopy: crescents and fibrin/fibrinoid necrosis.
  3. Three IF patterns: linear (anti-GBM), granular (immune complex), negative/minimal (pauci-immune).

Beyond source beyond source

  • RPGN is the clinical syndrome; crescentic glomerulonephritis is the pathologic picture. Dr. Kemp (nephrotic/nephritic lectures) treats RPGN as the severe end of nephritic syndrome.

2. Pathology Common to All RPGN

How a crescent forms

  1. Endothelial injury leads to a break (rupture) in the glomerular basement membrane (GBM).
  2. With the GBM broken there is no ultrafiltrate barrier: serum components, including large proteins such as fibrinogen, pour into Bowman space.
  3. The coagulation cascade is triggered in Bowman space; fibrinogen → fibrin.
  4. Fibrin stimulates parietal epithelial cells to proliferate, with macrophage infiltration, producing the cellular crescent.
Crescent: proliferating parietal epithelial cells and macrophages fill the urinary space and obliterate it around the compressed glomerular tuft. Often the majority of glomeruli have crescents.
Jones (silver) stain outlines the GBM; yellow arrows mark the breaks in it.

What each test shows

MethodFinding in RPGN
Light microscopyCrescents and fibrin deposition / fibrinoid necrosis. Same in all subtypes, so it can't tell them apart
Jones silver stainBreaks in the GBM
IF for fibrinogenCrescents are positive for fibrinogen/fibrin
IF for immunoglobulinDefines the subtype (Section 4)
EMRuptures in the GBM
Fibrinogen IF: the crescent lights up because fibrin is present in the crescent.
Don't confuseFibrinogen IF highlights the crescent in every subtype. The immunoglobulin stain (IgG linear / granular / none) is what differentiates them.

3. Prognosis and Treatment

  • Early diagnosis and early treatment are ideal because the disease progresses so fast.
  • Prognosis depends on the extent of crescentic/glomerular involvement on pathology.
Biopsy pattern5-year renal recovery after treatment
Focal lesions with >50% normal-appearing glomeruliFavorable: >90% recover
>50% of glomeruli globally sclerosed<25% recover

Treatment

  • High-dose steroids plus other immunosuppressants in all subtypes.
  • Anti-GBM disease: add plasmapheresis (first line, with immunosuppression) to remove the autoantibodies.
  • Immune complex RPGN: treat the underlying condition.
Beyond source beyond sourceCommonly used agents include cyclophosphamide and rituximab (ANCA disease also plasmapheresis in selected severe cases). Not discussed in the lecture.

4. The Three Subtypes by Immunofluorescence

SubtypeIFFrequencyUnderlying
Anti-GBM diseaseLINEAR IgG10–15% (least common)Autoantibody to α3 chain of type IV collagen (kidney ± lung)
Immune complexGRANULAR (IgG, IgM, IgA) along capillary walls25–30%Complication of immune-complex GN: post-infectious GN, lupus, IgA nephropathy, IgA vasculitis (HSP)
Pauci-immuneNEGATIVE / minimal40–50% (most common)ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis (80–90% ANCA-positive); renal-limited vasculitis

The percentages are his; they don't add to 100% in the lecture (the transcript acknowledges some subjectivity in reading IF). Pauci-immune means "few immune complexes."

Highest-yield memoryHe says how each subtype stains on IF is the single most important thing to commit to memory: linear = anti-GBM; granular = immune complex; none = pauci-immune/ANCA.

5. Anti-GBM RPGN (Goodpasture Syndrome)

FeatureDetail
Frequency10–15% of RPGN; <2 cases per million per year
PathogenesisCirculating IgG against an antigen intrinsic to the GBM and the alveolar basement membrane: the α3 chain of type IV collagen
Lung~50% have alveolar hemorrhage; kidney + lung = Goodpasture syndrome
CauseUsually unknown; associations: cigarette smoking, pulmonary infections
IFLinear IgG, "global linear staining" that uniformly outlines the glomerular capillary loops (the contour of the GBM)
TreatmentImmunosuppression + plasmapheresis
PrognosisPoor without treatment; death from renal failure and/or pulmonary hemorrhage
Antibody (anti-GBM) binds the basement membrane (illustration). IF: IgG, global linear staining.
Lung in Goodpasture syndrome: alveolar sacs filled with red blood cells (alveolar hemorrhage), which impairs gas exchange.
Test-worthy contrastGoodpasture: autoantibody against the α3 chain of type IV collagen. Alport syndrome: genetic mutation of the α5 chain of type IV collagen. Acquired antibody vs inherited defect.

6. Immune Complex RPGN

  • 25–30% of RPGN; second most common.
  • It is a complication of any immune-complex glomerular disease (it is secondary to them):
    • Post-infectious glomerulonephritis
    • Lupus nephritis
    • IgA nephropathy (formerly Berger disease; the name changed about 15 years ago but old texts still use it)
    • IgA vasculitis (formerly Henoch-Schönlein purpura, HSP)
  • IF: immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM, IgA) deposit in a granular ("grainy") pattern along the capillary wall.
  • Treatment and prognosis depend on the underlying disease.
Immune complex RPGN: granular staining.
Mechanism reminderImmune complexes get stuck in the glomerulus; granular IF reflects discrete clumps of complex. Anti-GBM, by contrast, coats the membrane evenly.

7. Pauci-Immune RPGN and ANCA

  • Most common RPGN subtype (40–50%).
  • 80–90% are ANCA-positive. Typically part of a small-vessel systemic vasculitis; a minority are renal-limited vasculitis.
  • IF: negative or minimal immunoglobulin. (He notes IF reading has some subjectivity: "no" vs "minimal staining.")
  • Light microscopy still shows crescents and fibrinoid necrosis.
Pauci-immune: no or minimal staining.

ANCA patterns (very testable)

p-ANCA (perinuclear; B) and c-ANCA (cytoplasmic; A) on neutrophils.
c-ANCA (cytoplasmic)p-ANCA (perinuclear)
TargetProteinase-3 (PR3)Myeloperoxidase (MPO)
Why the patternPR3 is only weakly cationic, so it disperses through the cytoplasmMPO is strongly cationic, so it clings to the negatively charged nucleus (nucleic acids) and outlines it
DiseaseGPA (majority)MPA (majority); EGPA (when positive)
Exam patternHe expects a vignette plus a c-ANCA or p-ANCA result, and you pick the disease. c → GPA; p → MPA (or EGPA).

Pathogenesis (incompletely understood)

Cytokines prime neutrophils so ANCA antigens reach the surface → ANCA activates neutrophils, which release factors that activate the alternative complement pathway → activated neutrophils adhere to vessel walls; plasma spills into the necrotic zone and coagulation produces fibrinoid necrosis and crescents. (Kidney Comics / Jennette & Nachman.)
  • ANCA triggers release of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), which contain the autoantigens MPO and PR3.
  • NETs damage endothelial cells and the glomerular capillaries and are thought to propagate the ANCA response.
  • ANCA also activates neutrophils and the alternative complement pathway (C3 generation).

8. Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA; Wegener)

FeatureDetail
DiseaseNecrotizing vasculitis of small to medium arteries with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation
ANCAMajority c-ANCA (a small percentage p-ANCA)
OrgansRespiratory (upper and lower) and renal most often; eyes, skin and nervous system too
Respiratory symptomsChronic rhinitis, epistaxis (nosebleeds), nonproductive cough, hemoptysis
RenalAcute hematuria, proteinuria, rising creatinine; renal involvement in about 80%
PathologyGranulomas: ill-defined, coalescing, with multinucleated giant cells / macrophages; vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis
GPA, lung. Left: granulomatous inflammation. Right: higher-power view of the vasculitis.
Don't forgetThe lung and vessel pictures show what the disease looks like outside the kidney. In the kidney you still see crescents and fibrin deposition.
Beyond source beyond sourceThe upper airway + lower airway + kidney triad is the classic board clue, with c-ANCA/PR3.

9. Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA)

FeatureDetail
DiseaseSmall-vessel necrotizing vasculitis; commonly glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis, other systemic capillary beds (GI tract, skin)
Key distinction from GPANo granulomatous inflammation; pulmonary capillaritis is present
ANCAMajority p-ANCA
Renal involvement~90%
Skin biopsyLeukocytoclastic vasculitis: neutrophils infiltrate small superficial dermal vessels; fragmented neutrophils ("nuclear dust"); vessel disrupted and blood leaks → palpable purpura
MPA, skin: leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Right (higher power): fragmented neutrophils (nuclear dust) and blood leaking into the dermis.
Palpable purpuraThe same physical finding you may recall from IgA vasculitis (HSP); here it comes from neutrophil-mediated vessel disruption.

10. Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA; Churg-Strauss)

FeatureDetail
DiseaseNecrotizing systemic vasculitis with asthma, eosinophilia and pulmonary involvement
Renal involvement~45% (much lower than GPA ~80% and MPA ~90%)
ANCA<50% positive; typically p-ANCA
PathologyLung and extrapulmonary sites (skin, heart, nerves, GI): prominent eosinophilic infiltrate, granulomatous reaction around necrotic foci, vasculitis with eosinophils
EGPA, lung. Left: granulomatous inflammation. Right: vasculitis with many eosinophils in the infiltrate.
The ANCA-vasculitis trioGPA: granulomas, upper airway, c-ANCA/PR3, ~80% renal. MPA: no granulomas, capillaritis, p-ANCA/MPO, ~90% renal. EGPA: asthma + eosinophils, p-ANCA in <50%, ~45% renal.

Prognosis and clinical pearls

TopicRemember
DiagnosisClinicopathologic: weeks-to-months renal decline + nephritic urinalysis → biopsy
CrescentParietal epithelial proliferation + macrophages; GBM rupture → fibrinogen → fibrin; often most glomeruli involved
PrognosisFocal, >50% normal glomeruli: >90% recover. >50% globally sclerosed: <25% recover. Treat early.
ProteinuriaUsually <3.5 g/24 h (non-nephrotic)
Alport vs Goodpastureα5 chain mutation (genetic) vs α3 chain autoantibody
